title: Your ten verses
hook: pick the verses that stayed with you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of the path, and your line was the same: the end of the path. Which picture from the book came back to you on its own? Day two hundred twenty-nine, and graduation week.
screen: `THE END OF THE PATH — THE END OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Think about the songs you know by heart. You never sat down to memorize most of them. They just stuck, because at some point they meant something to you, and now they come back at odd moments: in the shower, in the car, on a hard day. A book of verses works the same way. You've read four hundred twenty-three of them. Most will blur. But a handful have probably already stuck, and those are the ones that will come back when you need them. Today we go looking for them. Today: your ten verses.
screen: `SONGS YOU KNOW BY HEART.` → `THEY JUST STUCK.` → `A HANDFUL ALREADY HAVE.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada was made to be carried this way. For centuries, most people who knew it didn't own a copy. They knew verses: a few learned as children, a few heard in a teacher's talk, a few chanted at a festival. Monks might learn the whole book by heart; a grandmother might know six verses and live by them. Both count. So here's a way to find yours. First, walk back through the book in your mind, chapter by chapter. The twin verses: the mind comes first. And verse five, in Max Müller's English: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Earnestness, and the island no flood can overwhelm. The fletcher straightening the arrow. The bee that takes nectar and leaves the flower. The spoon that never tastes the soup. The deep, still lake. Conquering yourself, rather than a thousand others. Drop by drop, the water pot fills. The world seen as a bubble. Not to do evil, to do good, to purify the mind: the teaching of all the Buddhas. Overcoming anger by not-anger. The Buddhas only point the way. The forest, the elephant, the creeper, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf. Second, notice which ones tug at you. Not the ones you think you ought to pick, the ones that actually came back to you on some ordinary day. Third, write them down, in your own words if you like. There's no right list. Two people who read the same book will choose different verses, because they're living different lives. That's the point. A verse becomes yours when it has a job in your life.
screen: `CARRIED IN MEMORY, NOT ON SHELVES.` · `WALK BACK THROUGH THE CHAPTERS.` · `NOTICE WHICH ONES TUG.` · `WRITE THEM DOWN.` · then, large: `YOURS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, with something to write on nearby, and leave it for after the bell. For now, just breathe, and let the verses come to you rather than hunting for them. When one floats up, give it a small nod, and let it settle back. Don't count. Don't judge whether it's a good one. Some will surprise you. When the bell rings, write down the ones that came, and keep adding through the day until there are ten. The bell holds the time.
Your ten verses. The lines from the book that stuck, the ones with a job in your life: these are yours.
Your line: yours. Today, write down ten verses, in any words, and keep the list somewhere you'll see it. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists carry a few Dhammapada verses by heart rather than the whole book; teachers often give a single verse as a theme for reflection, and some people keep favorite verses written by a shrine or a desk.
